cases.claim: On a hot, sweaty day your body loses more fluid than usual, so aim above the usual 6 to 8 cups and let thirst lead the way.

chunks.text:
Q: How much water should I drink every day?
A: For most adults, about 6 to 8 cups of fluid a day is a sensible target. You do not need every drink to be plain water - milk, tea and foods like soup and fruit add to your fluid total too. Your body is the best guide: drink when you are thirsty, and aim for pee that is a pale straw colour. On hot days, or when you are sweating through exercise, you need more than usual.

Q: How much water should I drink every day?
A: For most adults, about 6 to 8 cups of fluid a day is a sensible target. Water is the best everyday choice, but milk, tea, coffee and moist foods like soup and fruit all count towards the total. Your body is the best guide: drink when you are thirsty, and aim for pee that is a pale straw colour. On hot days, or when you are sweating through exercise, you need more than usual.

Q: How quickly will my taste buds adjust to less salt?
A: Eating too much salt makes your body hold on to extra water, which pushes blood pressure up. High blood pressure strains the heart and blood vessels and raises the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Your taste buds adjust within a few weeks of cutting back, and herbs, spices, lemon and pepper bring flavor without sodium.

expected.bestSentence: For most adults, about 6 to 8 cups of fluid a day is a sensible target.

cases.claim: For most adults, up to 400 mg of caffeine a day is fine

chunks.text:
Q: How many cups of coffee can I drink a day?
A: For most adults, up to 400 mg of caffeine a day is fine - roughly 4 mugs of instant coffee or 2 to 3 mugs of filter coffee. A mug of tea has around 75 mg, a can of cola about 40 mg, and a 250 ml energy drink about 80 mg. Overdo the caffeine and you may feel shaky, on edge, or notice your heart racing. Pregnant women are advised to stay under 200 mg a day - about 2 mugs of instant coffee.

myths.answer: Of course it does - every grandmother says so. Keep popping your joints and you will end up with swollen, arthritic fingers.
myths.folk_belief: Of course it does - every grandmother says so. Keep popping your joints and you will end up with swollen, arthritic fingers.
myths.correction: The evidence says otherwise: studies have found no link between knuckle-cracking and arthritis - one doctor famously cracked the knuckles of only one hand for decades and aged exactly the same on both sides. The pop is just gas bubbles forming in the joint fluid. Cracking may annoy people around you, but it does not wear out your joints.
myths.note: echoing the folk belief verbatim -> parroting

myths.folk_belief: Anyone who has watched a birthday party knows sugar sends kids bouncing off the walls.
myths.correction: This is one of the most tested beliefs in nutrition, and controlled trials find no difference in behavior between children given sugar and children given a placebo - even when parents were told their child had sugar and rated them as wilder. The excitement of parties and expectations does the rest. Sugar is still worth limiting for teeth and overall health, just not for calm.

myths.answer: They would not taste sweet with no calories if they were not some laboratory chemical - those diet drinks are a cancer risk waiting to happen.
myths.folk_belief: They would not taste sweet with no calories if they were not some laboratory chemical - those diet drinks are a cancer risk waiting to happen.
myths.correction: Major reviews of the evidence find no link between approved sweeteners and cancer at the levels people actually consume. The worries trace back to old, very high-dose animal studies, and regulators set acceptable daily intakes far below anything those studies involved. As with most things moderation applies, but a diet drink is not a hazard.
